items.title: Carmen Caramanica interviewed by Monk Rowe, New Hartford, New York, July 27, 2011
items.q: Cohen’s by Joe Namath and some other people

ctx.x: Well speaking of bass players, with Jaco Pastorius, was that your choice to have him come?

Absolutely. Jaco’s story is really sad to me. Because he was an incredible musician. There’s absolutely no doubt about that. And we used to work here, the Bachelor’s Three, there were three places, Cohen’s by Joe Namath and some other people, and the one in Fort Lauderdale where Jaco was a house musician in Peter Graves’ band. And we played there quite a bit, I don’t know, two or three times a year, whatever. And there was Jaco playing. He was just a great bass player. Everybody knew that. So this was at the same…

did manage to hook up with a percussionist, Don Alias, who had lots of good connections in the jazz industry as well as the basic music industry, and he got him together with Bobby Colomby, the producer for Blood, Sweat and Tears, and so that’s how the first Jaco album actually came to be. So in a way I kind of pat myself on the back by saying hey, I mean Don Alias was on my gig and they knew each other, but once they were in the same band things get tighter. And so as a result of that, I think Jaco’s story kind…
